title: India Scraps Capital Gains Tax on Foreign Investment in Government Bonds. The Rupee Forced Its Hand.
excerpt: The cabinet approved an ordinance eliminating the 12.5% long-term capital gains tax and possibly the 20% withholding tax on interest — a dramatic bid to lure back foreign capital as the rupee hits record lows.
body:
India's cabinet has approved the elimination of capital gains tax on foreign portfolio investment in government bonds — an emergency measure designed to stem the worst capital flight the country has experienced in a generation.

The decision, reported by The Economic Times and confirmed through multiple sources, will be implemented via an ordinance amending the Income Tax Act, bypassing the parliamentary route to signal urgency. Foreign investors currently pay a 12.5 per cent long-term capital gains tax on listed shares and bonds held for more than 12 months. That levy on government securities is now gone.

The government is also considering removing the 20 per cent withholding tax on interest earned from government bonds, which would make Indian sovereign debt among the most tax-friendly in Asia for foreign holders.

## A Currency in Crisis

The timing is anything but coincidental. The rupee has fallen 13 per cent against the dollar since 2024 and six per cent in 2026 alone, its worst annual depreciation in nearly a decade. The Iran war, which has kept Brent crude above $95 a barrel for months, has hammered India's current account and drained foreign exchange reserves.

Foreign portfolio investors have pulled a staggering $28 billion from Indian equities this year, smashing 2025's record outflow of $18.9 billion. In the bond market, the story is marginally better — FPIs have maintained a net positive position of $1.4 billion — but the government wants dramatically more.

The calculation is straightforward. If foreign money will not stay in Indian stocks while global uncertainty persists, New Delhi needs to make its bond market irresistible. Government securities, backed by sovereign guarantee and offering yields above six per cent, become far more attractive when the tax burden on gains and interest income vanishes entirely.

## What It Means for NRI Investors

For non-resident Indians with investment portfolios that include Indian government debt, the change is immediately material. The 12.5 per cent capital gains tax and 20 per cent interest withholding have long been cited as reasons NRI investors preferred Singapore, Dubai, or US Treasury markets over Indian gilts.

The removal of these levies puts Indian sovereign bonds on a more competitive footing with markets that already offer tax-exempt or treaty-protected returns. NRIs investing through the Foreign Portfolio Investment route — as opposed to the NRE/NRO deposit route — stand to benefit directly.

Financial advisors expect renewed interest in fully accessible route bonds, a category the Reserve Bank of India designates for unlimited foreign participation. The RBI is separately expected to expand this list, opening more long-tenor securities to overseas buyers.

## The Bigger Picture

The tax cut arrives as the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee meets in Mumbai for its June policy review. Governor Sanjay Malhotra is expected to announce the rate decision on Friday, with nearly 80 per cent of economists in a Reuters poll predicting the repo rate will stay at 5.25 per cent.

But the rate decision and the tax cut are part of the same equation. India needs foreign capital flowing in, not out. The rate holds the cost of borrowing steady while the tax exemption sweetens the return on lending to the government.

The move also reflects a broader shift in India's approach to capital controls. For years, policymakers resisted the idea of competing on tax treatment for foreign bond investors, arguing that India's growth story and yield premium were enough. The Iran war, the rupee's slide, and the sheer scale of equity outflows have ended that debate.

India's Chief Economic Advisor V. Anantha Nageswaran warned in November that IPOs had "increasingly become exit vehicles for early investors rather than mechanisms for raising long-term capital." The same pattern — foreign money entering India only to leave — now threatens the bond market too. The tax exemption is designed to reverse that flow, or at least slow it.

Whether it works depends on something no ordinance can control: the trajectory of crude oil prices and the war that keeps them elevated.
author: Diaspora Desk
